title: Chapter 52 – Heng Moves
html:
[Red Ridge Clan – Zhao Heng]

Zhao Heng has not stood unaided for three hundred and ten days, and he has not forgotten a single one of them.

The servants think he has lost interest in the days. He has not. He has lost interest in everything else. He keeps the count in his head. It is the only thing he has ever been able to do without a servant. When the physician tells him the date, he nods. When the steward reads him the ledgers, he nods. And in the long gray hours between the dawn tonic and the noon one, lying in the great carved bed in the east chamber of Red Ridge Hall, with the shutters half drawn and a thin line of summer light lying across the quilt, he lies still and counts, in the dry exact voice of a man tallying a debt.

Three hundred and ten.

It was a spring day, the day it happened. A clean cold bright one. He had been standing at the foot of a stair, in a courtyard, laughing at something, and then a small boy had said a small thing, and the world had come apart. He does not remember the pain. He remembers a smell of burning hair. He remembers that his foundation, which he had spent thirty-one years building, stone by stone, in the long patient discipline of a man who has never once in his life been hurried, had cracked from crown to base, like a plate dropped on a flagstone floor, and that the sound it made inside him was a sound he has been hearing every night since.

He is a late Foundation cultivator. He was, a year ago, the second-strongest man within two hundred miles of the Sect's border. He has thirty years left, perhaps forty, if he is careful, and drinks the tonic, and does not cultivate, and does not hope.

He lies in the bed, and counts, and does not hope.

* * *

"Uncle."

It is his niece. She stands in the doorway with the light behind her, small and straight in a high-collared robe of dark red, and her right hand, the ruined one, wrapped in black silk to the wrist, is held a little away from her body, as it always is. Zhao Qian is still a child. She is the cleverest he has ever known and the least forgiving, and in the last year he has watched the first become a kind of blade and the second a kind of armor. She has stopped smiling. He has not noticed the day.

"Qian." He does not turn his head. "You have been at the wall again."

"The wall is where the news arrives."

"It arrives in the hall. At supper. In the ordinary way."

"The ordinary way is slow." She comes in. She does not sit. She stands at the foot of the bed and looks at him, with the cool level eyes of someone whose father taught her to read a ledger and her mother taught her to read a face. "Zhao Bei has come back."

He is silent for a moment.

"Alone?"

"With six men. He came in at dawn. He has been in the lower hall since, with the steward, and he will not speak to anyone." A pause. "Uncle, he lost thirty."

"He lost nine. Nineteen were taken, and released, and are on the road home." He closes his eyes. "I had it from the hawk an hour ago. It does not matter. Thirty, or nine. It is the same thing."

"And the granary?"

"Burned. Partly."

"And the refiner?"

"Alive."

She says nothing. The silence in the room is long and dry. Outside, a thin hot wind stirs the cedars in the courtyard, and a servant is sweeping the stair, with long careful strokes, as if there were something on it that he did not wish to disturb.

"Then Bei is a fool," says Qian, at last, in a voice like cut glass.

"Bei is a steward." He opens his eyes. "I sent him to do a thing I could not do myself. It was always going to fail. I only wished to see how."

She looks at him.

"I wished to see," says Heng, very gently, "what the hill would do when it was hurt."

* * *

It is not till evening that the visitor comes.

He comes on foot. That is the first odd thing. He does not ride, or take a sedan, or arrive in a cart with a banner. He walks up the long cedar avenue to the gate of Red Ridge Hall, in the last red of the sunset, a lean quiet man in a gray scholar's robe, with ink on his cuff and a stoop in his shoulders, and the gatekeeper does not know what to do with him. He is polite. He gives no name. He asks, in a soft pleasant voice, whether the Patriarch is at home, and if so whether he might have the honor of a quarter-hour.

It is Qian who brings him up.

She had been at the gate. She does not say why. She walks a pace ahead of the stranger, up the dark stair and along the long gallery, and does not look back, and when they reach the door of the east chamber she stops and says, very low, without turning her head: "Uncle will be tired. Please do not stay long."

"I shall try not to be a burden," says the man.

His voice is like warm water. It is the voice of a physician. It is the voice, thinks Qian, of a man who has never in his life been afraid of anything, and has long since stopped finding it interesting. She does not like it. She goes in ahead, and announces him, with a small stiff bow, and goes to stand by the window with her hands behind her back.

Heng has not moved. He lies in the bed, in the dusk, in the long light of one lamp, and regards the stranger with the narrow patient gaze of a man who has been studying visitors for forty years.

"You are not Red Ridge's friend," he says.

"No."

"You are not the Sect's."

"Not any longer." The man smiles. It is a gentle thing, a smile of great sweetness, and it does something odd to the air in the room. "I think you know who I am, Patriarch. I think you have been expecting me for some time. I only hope I have not been too slow."

"Mu."

"Elder Mu, if you will. It is an old habit." He bows, very slightly, from the waist, to the man in the bed. "I am sorry to find you so unwell. I have heard a great deal about your foundation. It is a very great pity."

* * *

They talk until the lamp burns low.

Lamps are brought, and not touched. Tea is poured, and goes cold in the cups. It is not a conversation Qian will ever be able to reconstruct. She stands at the window with her good hand gripping the sill, and listens, and the two men's voices rise and fall in the dark like water in a pipe. There is no hurry in them. There is no threat. They discuss, in careful murmurs, the weather, the harvest, a mutual acquaintance in the Ford, the price of millet in the south. They discuss the Sect, and its recent pettiness, and the shocking decline of the Outer Court's standards. They discuss, at some length, the question of a certain hill.

He is not a man who threatens, she thinks. He is a man who waits.

It is the second hour before Mu says, quite lightly, as one mentions a small kindness: "I understand you have a physician who gives you the white tonic."

"Daily."

"It does not work."

Heng's face does not change. "It is not meant to work. It is meant to prevent a thing from becoming worse."

"A noble aim." The soft voice does not alter. "In my experience, Patriarch, a foundation that has been cracked cannot be prevented. It can be mended. Or it can be lost." A small pause. "I have had some experience of the second. I have a master, who is dying of it, in a cold cell not very far from here. He has been dying for eleven years. I have watched him do it. It is not a thing I recommend."

"And the first?"

"Is rather more interesting." Mu smiles. "There is a method. It is not a method of the Sect, or the Outer Court, or any of the old houses. It is very old. It uses blood. I will not pretend that it is a clean one." He lifts one pale hand, and with a finger traces, in the air, a thin curved line. "A cracked foundation is a bowl with a flaw in it. The standard physician pours more water in and hopes. I would take a little of something else. Something warm. Something that has been taken from a man who was strong, and does not need it any more. And I would pour it into the crack."

"And it would hold?"

"For a time."

"How long?"

"I am told," says Mu, "that the longest recorded case is eighty years."

The silence in the room is perfectly still.

Qian's fingers have gone white on the sill. She turns her head. She sees her uncle's face, in the half dark, and for one brief second, in the thin lamplight, she sees something in it that she has not seen in three hundred and ten days. It is naked. It is raw. It is, she thinks, a hunger so enormous that it has no name.

He knew, she thinks. He came to Red Ridge, because he knew what Uncle would want.

"And the price?" says Heng.

* * *

"A small one," says Mu.

He has risen, and gone to the window, and stands looking out at the dark cedars with his hands folded behind him. The last red light is fading from the sky. A single star shows, over the black line of the northern ridge, very bright and cold.

"I want what you want. The hill."

"The hill is nothing."

"I agree. It is a poor, thin, dying thing, with a vein that has not breathed in a decade. I would not give a copper for its soil." The gray back does not move. "But it has a door."

Heng says nothing.

"You know it has. You have known for a year. It was the reason for the Mirror, and the boy, and the tea. I do not ask how you came to suspect it. I ask only that you think about what you want. You want your foundation. You want the Lin clan humbled, and the Patriarch's boy dead, and the sleeping-room of the Founder open to your hands." A small dry pause. "You are not interested in the door itself. I am. I have a use for it. It is the lock of a vault, and the vault is under a pool, and the pool is the whole of my life's work."

"And what is under the pool?"

"Something that will not interest you at all." The faintest trace of a smile. "A very old man's last wish. I have no intention of telling you. I only ask that when the door is opened, it is I who walks through it first."

"And what do I get?"

"The hill. Every stone. Every herb, every pill, every ounce of iron in the refiner's forge. The boy's head, if you wish it. The Lin Patriarch's, in a box. I will not take a coin of it." Mu turns, at last, and his dark mild eyes rest on the man in the bed. "And I will cure you. With my own hand. In your own bed. The night before the siege."

Nobody speaks. In the corner, the lamp gutters.

"That is a very good offer," says Heng, slowly.

"I am a very patient man. I do not make poor ones."

"And what is the catch?"

"I told you I should not lie to you." Mu bows. "The method will need a donor. Someone strong, and young, and not entirely unwilling." A little silence. "I should not have mentioned it. It is the ugliest part. I find I am ashamed to name it."

"Who?"

"I have not decided." The gentle voice does not change. "But I will say that the choice, when it is made, will be yours."

* * *

When the visitor has gone, they sit a long time without speaking.

It is a heavy, awkward, breathless sort of silence. Qian has not left the window. Heng has not moved. In the bed, in the guttering lamplight, he lies with his eyes on the ceiling and his hands folded on his chest, as still as a man laid out for burial.

"You will not do it," says Qian.

"I have not said I will."

"You are thinking of it."

"I am thinking," says Heng, "of a great many things." He turns his head, slowly. His face, in the lamp, is gray and drawn and very old. "Qian. Come here."

She comes. She stands by the bed with her ruined hand held away from her body, in its black silk, and her chin up, and her eyes very bright.

"You are afraid," he says.

"I am not."

"You are. I can see it. You are afraid of what he is. And you are right." His voice is faint. "He is a very dangerous man. He is the sort of man who gives away what he does not mean to keep. I have known two or three. They are the only kind I have ever feared." A thin dry cough. "But I find I am more afraid of the other thing."

"What other thing?"

"Of dying in this bed, in a house on a ridge, an old man long before his time, having done nothing but count."

She does not answer. The wind stirs the cedars.

"They broke it, Qian," says Heng. It is almost a whisper. "A child broke it. A boy of seventeen years old, with a face like a stone, in a courtyard, in front of my whole house. I have lain here three hundred and ten days, and I have thought of every kind of vengeance there is, and none of them was enough. And now a man walks in at my gate and says: I can give you the hill, and the boy, and eighty years." The thin lips curl. "I find I am not a very good man."

"You are not a stupid man."

"No." He closes his eyes. "I am not. I know exactly what it will cost. I know that Mu will take what he wants from that door and leave me a husk. I know that when it is finished there will be nothing left of Red Ridge but a hall and a tomb. And I know that I shall say yes."

"Uncle—"

"I am tired, Qian." He opens his eyes. The two dark pools look up at her, very steady, very still. "I want to see it. I want to see it burn. I want to see the boy's face. Is that a sin?"

She looks at him. There is, for a long moment, nothing in her face at all.

"Yes," she says, at last. "I think it is."

"Then I shall commit it. And you will help me."

"Will I?"

"You have a hand that does not work," says Heng, very softly. "And a debt that you have not paid. I think you will."

She does not answer. She has gone, quite suddenly, white to the lips. But after a time, in the thick hush of the room, she bows, a short stiff bow, and says in a voice like cold iron:

"Yes, Uncle."

* * *

Zhao Bei is waiting in the lower hall, on his knees, when Heng is carried down at first light.

They have put the Patriarch in a chair of black lacquer, with a fur across his knees, and four bearers, and Qian walking behind with a lamp. It is a performance, and he knows it. He has not been downstairs in a month. He has dressed for it, in a robe of dark red silk, and let them comb his hair. A man who cannot stand may at least be made to look like a thing that has chosen to sit.

The steward does not look up. He is on both knees on the flagstones, with his shaved head bowed and his heavy hands flat on his thighs. His leather is scorched. There is a long raw burn across one cheek. For ten years Zhao Bei has been the hall's right hand, the one man whom the servants fear and the guards obey, and he kneels now as a farm hand kneels before a landlord.

"Patriarch," he says. "I have no excuse."

"No. You have not." The chair is set down. "Get up."

"I should prefer—"

"I did not ask what you preferred."

Bei gets up. He is a big man, and the movement is slow, and Heng watches him with the tired, dry attention of a man watching the last of a long sum come out. He is not angry. It is an odd thing to find, after three hundred and ten days. The anger has gone somewhere. He thinks that Mu took it, in the lamplight, with his warm kind hands.

"Tell me about the tunnel," he says.

"It was a trap."

"I assumed. Tell me how."

The steward wets his lips. "It was singing, sir."

"I beg your pardon?"

"The roof." The heavy face works. "I had never heard it. I was at the head of the line, with my hand on the wall, and thirty men behind me, and the vault above us was perfectly still. I have been in a hundred tunnels. I know what a dead one sounds like. This was not dead. There was a note." He swallows. "It came up from the floor. It was low, like a drone-pipe. It made my teeth ache. And my first thought was, that is a very clever acoustic. My second was to run."

"And you ran."

"I ran. And behind me the whole thing fell." Bei closes his eyes. "I did not look back. I want you to know that I did not look. I have a wife. I have four children. I thought, if I turn, I will be killed, and who will tell the Patriarch?"

"I see."

"It was the boy," says Bei, quietly.

Heng's fingers go still on the fur.

"There was a child in the granary, sir. I did not see him. But I felt something, as I ran, on the back of my neck. A cold finger. Like an eye." The steward's voice is flat. "I have been a Qi Refining ninth-stage for ten years, Patriarch. I have been hunted by a Pool-stage cultivator in the Ashen Reaches. I have never been so afraid in my life as I was in that tunnel, with nothing behind me but a sound."

"A nineteen-year-old boy," says Qian, from the doorway. Her voice is perfectly even.

"I did not say he was a boy. I said it felt like an eye." Bei looks round. His face is gray. "Young mistress, I do not know what is living on that hill. I do not think anyone does. But I will tell you this. It does not use a sword."

Heng is silent for a long time.

"And the friend?"

"I did not see him. I had the map from the letter. He sent a runner, three nights before." Bei's mouth tightens. "A boy of fourteen, with a Lin armband. He did not give his name. He had a gold ring."

"A signet?"

"It was the three-farms ring." The steward's eyes come up. "The Elder's."

It is very quiet in the hall. The lamp is guttering; the dawn is a thin pale line at the high windows. Heng lies in his chair with the fur across his knees and his hand lying open on it, and he does not smile. It is not a thing he will let himself do. But something moves in the hollow of his chest, very small and very cold. It is the long slow loosening of a clenched fist.

"I see," says Heng. "Thank you, Bei. You may go and sleep."

"Patriarch—"

"I am not displeased." He lifts one hand, wearily. "I am, on the whole, encouraged. A man who has run from a sound has learned something that I did not know. Go. We shall want you again, at the new moon."

The steward bows, a long stiff bow, and leaves. His footsteps recede along the flagstones, heavy and slow.

Qian has not moved.

"Uncle," she says, "you are going to use him."

"I am going to use everything." His eyes are closed. "That is what the cure is for."

She looks at him a moment longer. In the bleak gray light he seems already half a stranger, a thing of bone and silk and appetite, and she thinks, with a clarity that frightens her, of the small boy at the foot of the courtyard stair, a year ago, with his flat quiet eyes. She had hated him. She finds, to her distaste, that she no longer entirely does. It is a very uncomfortable thing to realize, standing in a great cold hall, that one has begun to wish to be on the other side of a door.

* * *

The letter goes out that same morning.

It is a small thing. A single sheet, folded in three, sealed with a plain gray wax and no crest, and given to a boy on a fast pony with orders to put it into no hand but the one named. The boy does not know the name. He is told only that the man lives in the old east house of the Lin hill, in a room that looks on the western farms, and that he will be waiting at a gate.

It says, in Heng's own cramped, gentle, unhurried script:

My friend,

Your last report was most valuable. I regret that my steward was unable to make better use of it. He is a blunt instrument. I shall not use him again.

The Blood Shadow has agreed to our arrangement. They will move on the new moon of the seventh month. I should like you to ensure that, on that night, the western gate of your clan's hall is not barred. You need not open it. It is only necessary that it not be locked.

In return, your three farms shall be exempt from the tribute of the Sect, and your family will be named in the Register of the Red Ridge, as a house of the second rank. You will not be harmed. I give you my word.

I am, with the highest regard,

Zhao Heng.

P.S. Give my compliments to your Patriarch. And tell him, if you can bring yourself to, that I have never been so interested in anyone.

He seals it with his own hand. Then he lies back among the pillows, in the pale morning light, with the cedars rustling, and in the stillness, for the first time in three hundred and eleven days, he does not count.

Down in the courtyard, a small figure in dark red stands in the thin early sun, looking up at his window. She has not been to bed. Her face is quite blank. After a long while she raises her ruined hand, in its black silk glove, and, very slowly, as if it were an unfamiliar thing, she makes a fist.
